implementation_notes: Ruby's privacy is method-level and advisory: `private`/`protected` keep writers away from explicit receivers, but `instance_variable_set`, `send` and `instance_variable_get` still reach the state, and `Module#private` marks methods, never data. The read-only surface is therefore built from `attr_reader` - a getter with no writer - plus `Object#freeze`, which makes further modification raise `FrozenError`; freezing must be applied once `initialize` has finished, typically by calling `freeze` at the end of the constructor or by using a `Data.define` value object, and it is shallow, so nested collections need freezing too. A holder class is worth it when several attributes form one invariant: a small frozen `Data`-derived class keeps them together and gives value equality.
code_sketch:
CircleData = Data.define(:radius)          # frozen value object (Ruby 3.2+)

class Circle
  def initialize(radius)
    @data = CircleData.new(radius: radius).freeze
  end

  def radius = @data.radius                 # reader only, no writer
end
pitfalls: `freeze` is shallow and `dup`/`clone` return unfrozen copies (clone may preserve frozen state only with `freeze: true`), so freeze the nested objects or build the holder from already-frozen values.
`instance_variable_set`, `send(:writer)` and reopening the class with a new writer defeat every `private` marker, so the guarantee is accidental-write protection, not encapsulation enforcement.

Freezing the holder does not stop the class from reassigning the `@data` variable itself; making the holder frozen only protects its contents, so assignment must be avoided by discipline or an explicit re-assignment method that creates a new object.
